Section 3(p) - an invention which in effect, is traditional knowledge or which is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known component or components. section: SECTION 64 - REVOCATION OF PATENTS
text:
The Patents Act, 1970 (Act No. 39 of 1970)
SECTION 64 - REVOCATION OF PATENTS
Authority: Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM), DPIIT
Jurisdiction: IN

Section 64(1) - Subject to the provisions contained in this Act, a patent, whether granted before or after the commencement of this Act, may, be revoked on a petition of any person interested or of the Central Government by the Appellate Board or on a counter-claim in a suit for infringement of the patent by the High Court on any of the following grounds, that is to say
Section 64(1)(a) - that the invention, so far as claimed in any claim of the complete specification, was claimed in a valid claim of earlier priority date contained in the complete specification of another patent granted in India;
Section 64(1)(b) - that the patent was granted on the application of a person not entitled under the provisions of this Act to apply therefor;
Section 64(1)(e) - that the invention so far as claimed in any claim of the complete specification is not an invention within the meaning of this Act, or is not patentable under this Act;
Section 64(1)(f) - that the complete specification does not sufficiently and fairly describe the invention and the method by which it is to be performed, i.e., that the description of the method or the instructions for the working of the invention as contained in the complete specification are not by themselves sufficient to enable a person in India possessing average skill in, and average knowledge of, the art to which the invention relates, to work the invention, or that it does not disclose the best method of performing it which was known to the applicant for the patent and for which he was entitled to claim protection;
Section 64(1)(q) - that the complete specification does not disclose or wrongly mentions the source and geographical origin of biological material used for the invention;
Section 64(1)(r) - that the invention so far as claimed in any claim of the complete specification is anticipated having regard to the knowledge, oral or otherwise, available within any local or indigenous community in India or elsewhere.
PRACTICAL GUIDANCE: PATENTING AYURVEDIC INNOVATIONS
TKDL (Traditional Knowledge Digital Library): The TKDL is a collaborative project between the Ministry of AYUSH and CSIR. It contains over 900 traditional Ayurvedic formulations transcribed from ancient Sanskrit/Hindi texts into modern classification systems. Patent examiners worldwide use TKDL to identify prior art and reject patent applications that merely attempt to patent traditional knowledge.
Patentable subject matter in Ayurveda: Innovations in Ayurveda may be patentable if they demonstrate:
1. A novel delivery mechanism not previously known (e.g., nanoparticle encapsulation of an Ayurvedic herb extract)
2. A new synergistic combination effect scientifically proven beyond the sum of individual parts
3. A novel extraction process that yields a substance with demonstrably different efficacy
4. A novel formulation with a new therapeutic indication not previously known
Non-patentable subject matter in Ayurveda:
1. Classical Ayurvedic formulations as described in Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, or Ashtanga Hridayam
2. Mere admixtures of known herbs without proven synergistic effect
3. Traditional preparations described in Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India
4. Known formulations with only slight modifications without enhanced efficacy

GEOGRAPHICAL INDICATIONS OF GOODS ACT 1999 - KEY PROVISIONS
Section 2(e) - "geographical indication" means an indication which identifies such goods as agricultural goods, natural goods or manufactured goods as originating, or manufactured in the territory of a country, or a region or locality in that territory, where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of such goods is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and in case where such goods are manufactured goods one of the activities of either the production or of processing or preparation of the goods concerned takes place in such territory, region or locality, as the case may be.
GI Registration for Ayurveda Products:
Several Ayurvedic products have received Geographical Indication (GI) registration in India. GI registration protects traditional Ayurvedic products that are produced in specific geographical regions and have qualities attributable to their origin. Examples include:
1. Mysore Agarbathi - GI Tag: Incense sticks from Mysore with traditional formulation
2. Mahabaleshwar Honey - Regional honey with specific properties
3. Coorg Cardamom - Cardamom from Kodagu district with specific aroma profile
4. Kashmir Saffron (Kesar) ? GI Tag 2020 - Known for high crocin content
GI vs Trademark for Ayurvedic Products:
- GI protects a community of producers in a region (e.g., all Chyawanprash manufacturers in a specific region following classical Ayurvedic formulation)
- Trademark protects a specific brand name of an individual manufacturer
- Both can coexist: A manufacturer can have a trademark brand name for their product while the underlying formula has GI protection
- GI registration does NOT prevent others in the same region from using the geographical indication
- TKDL documentation can be used to support GI applications for ancient formulations
PRACTICAL GUIDANCE: TRADEMARK STRATEGY FOR AYURVEDA BRANDS
Step 1 - Clearance Search: Conduct a search on the Indian Trade Marks Registry (https://ipindiaservices.gov.in) before filing. Search for identical and phonetically similar marks in the relevant class.
Step 2 - Class Selection: For Ayurvedic products
- Class 5: Pharmaceutical preparations, medicinal herbs, dietary supplements
- Class 29: Food products, dairy products, ghee
- Class 30: Spices, condiments, food flavorings, herbal teas
- Class 32: Non-alcoholic beverages, herbal drinks
- Class 44: Medical services, Ayurvedic treatment services
Step 3 - Distinctiveness: Generic Ayurvedic ingredient names (e.g., "Ashwagandha", "Triphala") cannot be registered as trademarks. Distinctive brand names that are coined, arbitrary, or fanciful are preferred.
Step 4 - Filing: Applications can be filed online through IP India portal. Fee for application: Rs. 4,500 per class (e-filing, natural person/startup/small enterprise) or Rs. 9,000 per class (other entities).
Step 5 - Opposition Period: After examination and acceptance, the mark is advertised in the Trade Marks Journal for 4 months. Any party may oppose registration during this period.
Step 6 - Registration Certificate: Upon expiry of opposition period without opposition (or after successful defence), the trademark registration certificate is issued. Valid for 10 years, renewable indefinitely.

text:
Food Safety and Standards (Ayurveda Aahara) Regulations, 2022
CHAPTER 5 - LICENSING AND REGISTRATION
Authority: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)
Jurisdiction: IN

Regulation 5.1 - All manufacturers of Ayurveda Aahara products shall obtain a license under the Food Safety and Standards (Licensing and Registration of Food Businesses) Regulations, 2011 before commencing manufacturing operations.
Regulation 5.2 - In addition to FSSAI licensing, manufacturers who wish to make Rasayana or Bhasma-containing products shall also obtain a No-Objection Certificate from the State Licensing Authority under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.
Regulation 5.3 - Products containing Schedule E(1) herbs (potentially toxic herbs) as listed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act shall require prior approval from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).
PRACTICAL GUIDANCE: FSSAI COMPLIANCE FOR AYURVEDA PRODUCTS
Step 1 - Product Classification: Determine whether your product is an Ayurveda Aahara (food) or an Ayurvedic medicine (drug). If therapeutic claims are intended, the product must be licensed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act as an Ayurvedic proprietary medicine, not as food.
Step 2 - Ingredient Verification: Check all ingredients against Schedule I (permitted) and Schedule II (prohibited). Any ingredient not listed requires prior FSSAI approval.
Step 3 - Label Review: Ensure all mandatory label information is present. Health claims must reference classical Ayurvedic texts or peer-reviewed literature.
Step 4 - Testing Requirements: Heavy metal testing by NABL-accredited laboratory. Microbial testing as per FSS regulations. Pesticide residue testing for all herb-based ingredients.
Step 5 - Licensing: Apply for Central or State FSSAI license depending on annual turnover. Annual turnover below Rs. 12 lakhs - State registration. Annual turnover Rs. 12 lakhs to Rs. 20 crores - State license. Annual turnover above Rs. 20 crores - Central license.

Section 2(1)(zb) & 2(1)(m) - Statutory Definitions of Trademark and Mark
Authority: Trade Marks Registry, CGPDTM, Ministry of Commerce and Industry
Jurisdiction: IN

Under Section 2(1)(zb) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a 'trade mark' means a mark capable of being represented graphically and which is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others and may include shape of goods, their packaging and combination of colours. Section 2(1)(m) defines 'mark' to include a device, brand, heading, label, ticket, name, signature, word, letter, numeral, shape of goods, packaging or combination of colours or any combination thereof. In Ayurvedic commerce, trade dress, bottle silhouettes, and brand names (e.g., 'Zandu', 'Baidyanath') function as protected marks, whereas generic herbal names cannot be monopolized.

Section 9 - Absolute Grounds for Refusal of Descriptive Herbal Terms
Authority: Trade Marks Registry, CGPDTM, Ministry of Commerce and Industry

Section 9(1) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 prohibits the registration of trademarks which: (a) Are devoid of any distinctive character; (b) Consist exclusively of marks or indications which may serve in trade to designate the kind, quality, intended purpose, values, geographical origin, or time of production of goods. Application in Ayurvedic Products: Common Sanskrit names of plants (e.g., 'Ashwagandha', 'Brahmi', 'Triphala', 'Tulsi', 'Neem') cannot be registered as trademarks in Class 5 (Pharmaceuticals/Herbal Medicines) or Class 30 (Dietary Foods) because they are generic and publici juris. Any manufacturer is legally entitled to describe their product using these botanical terms.

Authority: Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) & Ministry of Ayush

Under Section 3(a) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, 'Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani (ASU) drug' includes all medicines intended for internal or external use for or in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease or disorder in human beings or animals, and manufactured exclusively in accordance with formulae described in authoritative books of Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani systems of medicine specified in the First Schedule. The First Schedule explicitly recognizes 54 classical texts as statutory benchmarks, including Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, Ashtanga Sangraha, Ashtanga Hridaya, Sharangadhara Samhita, Bhavaprakasha, Bhaishajya Ratnavali, Sahasrayogam, and the Ayurvedic Formulary of India (AFI). Medicines manufactured strictly per these 54 texts are classified as 'Classical ASU Medicines' requiring no clinical trials.

Rule 158B - Licensing Requirements for Classical vs Patent & Proprietary ASU Drugs
Authority: Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) & Ministry of Ayush
Jurisdiction: IN

Rule 158B of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 specifies regulatory evidentiary requirements for grant of manufacturing licenses for Ayurvedic, Siddha, or Unani medicines: (I) Classical ASU Medicines (Form 24D / Form 25D): Manufactured in strict accordance with formulae described in authoritative books in the First Schedule. Requires proof of textual citation, authentic raw material verification, and Schedule T GMP compliance. No clinical trials or safety toxicity studies are mandated. (II) Patent or Proprietary (P&P) ASU Medicines (Rule 158B(II)): Formulations containing ASU ingredients but in novel combinations, ratios, or delivery forms. Licensees must submit published safety literature, pilot clinical trials, and stability data. (III) Standardized Extracts / Phytopharmaceuticals: Complete chromatographic fingerprinting, active marker assays, and toxicology are mandatory.

Schedule T - Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) for ASU Medicines
Authority: Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) & Ministry of Ayush
Jurisdiction: IN

Schedule T of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 establishes Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) that all licensed manufacturing units of Ayurvedic, Siddha, and Unani drugs must comply with: (1) Factory Premises: Location in hygienic surroundings, minimum space requirement (1,200 sq. ft. for basic manufacturing plus raw material, packaging storage, and finished goods quarantine). (2) Technical Staffing Mandate: Manufacturing must take place under the direct supervision of competent technical staff possessing either a recognized degree in Ayurvedic Medicine (BAMS) or Ayurvedic Pharmacy (B.Pharm Ayurveda) from a recognized university. (3) Quality Control Laboratory: Must have facilities for physical testing (moisture, total ash, acid-insoluble ash), chemical analysis (TLC/HPTLC profiling, assay of active markers), heavy metal testing (Pb, Cd, Hg, As), and microbial limits. (4) Batch Manufacturing Records (BMR): Complete manufacturing and analytical records must be retained for 3 years or 1 year past expiry date.

Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940: Section 33EE: An Ayurvedic, Siddha, or Unani drug shall be deemed to be adulterated if it consists in whole or part of filthy, putrid, or decomposed substances, or if colored with unprescribed dyes, or substituted with foreign matter. Under the ABS Regulations 2014 framed under Section 21 of the Biological Diversity Act: Commercial Utilization Benefit Sharing Percentages on Ex-Factory Sale Price: (a) Annual gross ex-factory sale of product up to Rs. 1,00,00,000: 0.1% of sales. (b) Annual gross ex-factory sale between Rs. 1,00,00,001 and Rs. 3,00,00,000: 0.2% of sales. (c) Annual gross ex-factory sale exceeding Rs. 3,00,00,000: 0.5% of sales. Alternatively, buyers may opt for 3.0% to 5.0% of the purchase price of the biological resource. For IPR/Patents: If the applicant commercializes the patent himself, 0.2% to 1.0% of ex-factory sale price; if licensed or assigned to a third party, 3.0% to 5.0% of license fee and 2.0% to 5.0% of ongoing royalty.

authority: Ministry of Ayush, CDSCO & FSSAI Advisory
section: Selling Ayurvedic Products Without a Patent: The Direct-to-Consumer (D2C) Commercial Reality
text:
Commercialization of Ayurvedic Products Without Patents: D2C Licensing & Compliance
Selling Ayurvedic Products Without a Patent: The Direct-to-Consumer (D2C) Commercial Reality
Authority: Ministry of Ayush, CDSCO & FSSAI Advisory
Jurisdiction: IN

Do you need a patent to manufacture, sell, or commercialize an Ayurvedic product? The definitive legal answer is NO. A patent is merely a 20-year negative right allowing an inventor to exclude others from commercially making or selling a novel, non-obvious technological invention. A patent is never a license, permit, or legal prerequisite to enter the market or sell directly to consumers. In practice, more than 85% of all Ayurvedic medicines, cosmetics, and wellness products sold in India and globally (by leading enterprises such as Dabur, Baidyanath, Himalaya, Forest Essentials, Kottakkal Arya Vaidya Sala, and emerging D2C brands) are commercialized without patents. Classical formulations (such as Chyawanprash, Triphala, Ashwagandharishta, Kumkumadi Taila, and Mahabhringraj Oil) cannot be patented under Section 3(p) of the Patents Act, 1970 because they are documented in First Schedule texts and constitute prior art in the public domain. Entrepreneurs can freely manufacture, package, market, and sell these classical formulations directly to consumers, provided they obtain the mandatory statutory licenses from the State Licensing Authority (SLA) or FSSAI.
source: Ministry of Ayush, CDSCO & FSSAI Advisory

title: Commercialization of Ayurvedic Products Without Patents: D2C Licensing & Compliance
authority: Ministry of Ayush, CDSCO & FSSAI Advisory
section: Mandatory Licensing Requirements to Sell Directly to Consumers (Form 25D & Schedule T GMP)
text:
Commercialization of Ayurvedic Products Without Patents: D2C Licensing & Compliance
Mandatory Licensing Requirements to Sell Directly to Consumers (Form 25D & Schedule T GMP)
Authority: Ministry of Ayush, CDSCO & FSSAI Advisory
Jurisdiction: IN

To manufacture and sell Ayurvedic products directly to consumers legally without a patent, a business must comply with the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 by obtaining one of the following manufacturing licenses from the State Licensing Authority (AYUSH): (1) Classical / Shastric Formulation License (Form 25D): For products manufactured strictly following the exact recipe, ingredients, and processes prescribed in any of the 54 First Schedule authoritative texts. No animal toxicology or clinical efficacy trials are legally mandated; submission of the textual citation from classical treatises is sufficient for approval. (2) Patent or Proprietary (P&P) Medicine License (Form 25D / Rule 158B): For formulations containing ingredients mentioned in First Schedule texts but formulated in modern convenient dosage forms (capsules, effervescent tablets, syrups) or novel ratios. Requires safety data (acute oral toxicity per Rule 158B), stability data, and heavy metal testing. (3) Loan License (Form 25E) or Contract Third-Party Manufacturing: Startups and D2C brands do not need to build their own manufacturing plants. They can legally manufacture their branded Ayurvedic formulations via GMP-certified third-party or loan-license facilities. (4) Schedule T Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP): Every Ayurvedic manufacturing unit must comply with Schedule T requirements regarding infrastructure, sanitation, batch manufacturing records, quality control labs, and heavy metal testing limits (Lead <= 10 ppm, Arsenic <= 3 ppm, Cadmium <= 0.3 ppm, Mercury <= 1 ppm).
source: Ministry of Ayush, CDSCO & FSSAI Advisory

section: The FSSAI Ayurveda Aahara Direct-to-Consumer Alternative for Wellness Products
text:
Commercialization of Ayurvedic Products Without Patents: D2C Licensing & Compliance
The FSSAI Ayurveda Aahara Direct-to-Consumer Alternative for Wellness Products
Authority: Ministry of Ayush, CDSCO & FSSAI Advisory
Jurisdiction: IN

Entrepreneurs who do not wish to operate under pharmaceutical drug regulations can commercialize their formulations under the Food Safety and Standards (Ayurveda Aahara) Regulations, 2022. Scope & Advantages: Covers foods, food supplements, herbal beverages, and nutritional formulations prepared according to classical Ayurvedic recipes or using botanicals recognized in authoritative texts. Products are licensed via the online FoSCoS portal without requiring a pharmaceutical AYUSH drug license. Direct-to-Consumer Retail: Ayurveda Aahara products can be sold over-the-counter and through modern e-commerce channels directly to general consumers. Mandatory Labeling & Regulatory Boundaries: All products must prominently display the official green 'Ayurveda Aahara' logo. Products cannot be labeled or marketed as drugs, cannot claim to diagnose, treat, mitigate, or cure any specific disease, and must carry the disclaimer that the product is not intended as a medicinal substitute.
source: Ministry of Ayush, CDSCO & FSSAI Advisory

authority: Ministry of Ayush, CDSCO & FSSAI Advisory
section: Protecting Brand Equity and Commercial Assets Without Patents (Trademarks & Trade Secrets)
text:
Commercialization of Ayurvedic Products Without Patents: D2C Licensing & Compliance
Protecting Brand Equity and Commercial Assets Without Patents (Trademarks & Trade Secrets)
Authority: Ministry of Ayush, CDSCO & FSSAI Advisory
Jurisdiction: IN

When product formulations cannot be patented due to Section 3(p) (traditional knowledge) or Section 3(e) (mere admixture), D2C Ayurvedic companies protect and maximize their enterprise value through alternative intellectual property mechanisms: (1) Trademark Protection (The Trade Marks Act, 1999): Brands protect their unique trade names, logos, slogans, and trade dress packaging. Section 13 Precaution: Descriptive Ayurvedic names (e.g. 'Ashwagandha', 'Triphala', 'Brahmi', 'Taila') cannot be registered as trademarks because they are generic public names. However, distinctive arbitrary coined names (e.g. 'Kama Ayurveda', 'Kapiva', 'Baidyanath Chyawan-Fit') are fully registerable under Class 5 (medicines/herbal supplements) and Class 3 (herbal cosmetics and skincare). (2) Trade Secrets & Proprietary Extraction Know-How: Companies protect proprietary extraction ratios, standardized extract percentages (e.g. Withanolides 5%), solvent temperature curves, and specialized taste-masking technologies under Common Law Trade Secret protection backed by robust employee and supplier Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs). (3) Advertising & Consumer Protection Compliance: Direct-to-consumer Ayurvedic sellers must strictly observe the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. It is a criminal offense to advertise miraculous or guaranteed cures for chronic diseases specified in the Schedule (such as diabetes, cancer, heart disease, blindness, or kidney failure).
source: Ministry of Ayush, CDSCO & FSSAI Advisory

title: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940: Section 33EE - Misbranded Ayurvedic Drugs
authority: Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) & Ministry of Ayush
section: Section 33EE
chapter: Chapter IV-A: Provisions Relating to Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani Drugs
text:
Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940: Section 33EE - Misbranded Ayurvedic Drugs
Section 33EE
Authority: Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) & Ministry of Ayush
Jurisdiction: IN

Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, Chapter IV-A, Section 33EE.
Statutory Definition of Misbranded Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani Drugs:
An Ayurvedic drug shall be deemed to be misbranded:—
(a) if it is so coloured, coated, powdered or polished that damage is concealed, or if it is made to appear of better or greater therapeutic value than it really is;
(b) if it is not labelled in the prescribed manner; or
(c) if its label or container or anything accompanying the drug bears any statement, design or device which makes any false claim for the drug or which is false or misleading in any particular.

Regulatory Enforceability: Selling, stocking, or manufacturing a misbranded Ayurvedic drug is an offence punishable under Section 33-I with imprisonment and fine.
source: Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) & Ministry of Ayush

title: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940: Section 33EEB - Patent or Proprietary Ayurvedic Medicine Definition
authority: Ministry of Ayush / State Licensing Authorities
section: Section 33EEB
text:
Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940: Section 33EEB - Patent or Proprietary Ayurvedic Medicine Definition
Section 33EEB
Authority: Ministry of Ayush / State Licensing Authorities
Jurisdiction: IN

Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, Chapter IV-A, Section 33EEB.
Statutory Definition:
'Patent or Proprietary medicine' in relation to Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani systems means a drug which is a remedy or prescription presented in a form ready for internal or external administration of human beings or animals and which is not included in the edition of the authoritative books specified in the First Schedule, but contains as ingredients only substances included in those books or the Pharmacopoeias.

Key Legal Implications:
1. Unlike a patent granted under the Patents Act 1970, an Ayurvedic 'Patent or Proprietary Medicine' under the Drugs & Cosmetics Act is merely a regulatory licensing category, not a monopoly patent right.
2. All ingredients must be strictly sourced from texts listed in the First Schedule to the Act.
source: Ministry of Ayush / State Licensing Authorities

Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, Part XVI, Rule 158B.
Regulatory Mandate for Patent or Proprietary ASU Medicines:
For the grant of a manufacturing license (Form 25D) for Ayurvedic Patent or Proprietary medicines, applicants must submit:
Category A (Classical ingredients with new indication or dosage):
- Published literature / textual references from First Schedule texts.
- Acute oral toxicity data.
Category B (New combination of classical ingredients):
- Safety data: Acute oral toxicity studies as per OECD guidelines.
- Proof of Efficacy: Evidence from published peer-reviewed journals or a pilot clinical trial conducted by a recognized clinical research organization.
Category C (Aqueous/hydroalcoholic extracts of classical ingredients):
- Heavy metal testing, pesticide residue testing, microbial load compliance, and batch standardization data.

Schedule T
Authority: Ministry of Ayush

Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, Schedule T (Good Manufacturing Practices for ASU Drugs).
Mandatory Requirements for Every ASU Drug Factory:
1. Location and Surroundings: Factory must be situated in hygienic conditions, free from open drains or contaminants.
2. Minimum Manufacturing Space: Standard minimum area prescribed for churna, tablet/vati, taila/ghrita, and asava/arishta sections.
3. Quality Control Section: Must maintain an in-house laboratory or tie-up with a government-approved laboratory for raw material identity testing, moisture content, total ash, microbial load, and heavy metal testing.

title: The Patents Act, 1970: Section 10(4)(ii)(D) - Disclosure of Biological Source and Origin
authority: Parliament of India / CGPDTM
section: Section 10(4)(ii)(D)
text:
The Patents Act, 1970: Section 10(4)(ii)(D) - Disclosure of Biological Source and Origin
Section 10(4)(ii)(D)
Authority: Parliament of India / CGPDTM
Jurisdiction: IN

The Patents Act, 1970, Chapter III, Section 10(4)(ii)(D).
Statutory Requirement:
Where an invention uses biological material, the applicant must disclose the source and geographical origin of the biological material in the complete specification (Form 2).

Consequences of Non-Disclosure or False Disclosure:
1. Ground of Opposition: Under Section 25(1)(j) and Section 25(2)(j), failure to disclose or wrongful disclosure of the geographical origin of biological material is a ground for pre-grant and post-grant opposition.
2. Ground of Revocation: Under Section 64(1)(p), a granted patent is liable to be revoked by the High Court if the complete specification does not disclose or wrongly mentions the source or geographical origin of biological materials.
source: Parliament of India / CGPDTM

title: The Patents Act, 1970: Section 3(e) - Exclusion of Mere Admixtures
authority: Parliament of India / Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM)
section: Section 3(e)
text:
The Patents Act, 1970: Section 3(e) - Exclusion of Mere Admixtures
Section 3(e)
Authority: Parliament of India / Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM)
Jurisdiction: IN

The Patents Act, 1970 (Act No. 39 of 1970), Chapter II, Section 3(e).
Statutory Text:
Section 3. What are not inventions — The following are not inventions within the meaning of this Act,—
(e) a substance obtained by a mere admixture resulting only in the aggregation of the properties of the components thereof or a process for producing such substance.

Statutory Interpretation for Ayurvedic and Herbal Innovations:
Under Indian Patent Office (IPO) Guidelines for Examination of Patent Applications in the Field of Pharmaceuticals and Traditional Knowledge:
1. When an applicant combines known medicinal herbs or extract fractions (such as Ashwagandha and Brahmi), the objection under Section 3(e) is mandatory.
2. To overcome this statutory bar, the applicant MUST submit comparative in-vitro bioassay or clinical pharmacological data proving unexpected SYNERGY (where the therapeutic activity of the mixture is statistically significantly higher than the sum of its individual parts).
3. If no quantitative synergy data is submitted in the complete specification (Form 2), the application will be refused under Section 15.
source: Parliament of India / Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM)

title: The Patents Act, 1970: Section 3(p) - Exclusion of Traditional Knowledge
authority: Parliament of India / CGPDTM
section: Section 3(p)
text:
The Patents Act, 1970: Section 3(p) - Exclusion of Traditional Knowledge
Section 3(p)
Authority: Parliament of India / CGPDTM
Jurisdiction: IN

The Patents Act, 1970, Section 3(p) (as inserted by Act 38 of 2002).
Statutory Text:
Section 3. What are not inventions —
(p) an invention which in effect, is traditional knowledge or which is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known component or components.

Examination Procedure:
- Patent examiners routinely conduct automated cross-searches against the CSIR-AYUSH Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL).
- If the claimed formulation, combination, or use is documented in classical texts of Ayurveda, Unani, or Siddha, the invention is barred under Section 3(p).
- Patentability can only be recognized if the applicant proves an inventive step beyond traditional knowledge (such as a novel standardized bioactive isolation process, a non-obvious drug delivery vehicle like phytosomes or nanoparticles, or a validated new therapeutic indication not disclosed in ancient texts).
source: Parliament of India / CGPDTM

title: National Biodiversity Authority: Guidelines for Prior Approval under Section 6 of Biological Diversity Act
authority: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), Chennai
section: Section 6 & Regulation 8 (Form III)
text:
National Biodiversity Authority: Guidelines for Prior Approval under Section 6 of Biological Diversity Act
Section 6 & Regulation 8 (Form III)
Authority: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), Chennai
Jurisdiction: IN

Biological Diversity Act, 2002, Section 6(1) & NBA Guidelines.
Mandatory Statutory Requirement:
No person shall apply for any intellectual property right, by whatever name called, in or outside India for any invention based on any research or information on a biological resource obtained from India without obtaining the prior approval of the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA).

Form III Procedure & Timing:
1. Indian Applicants: May apply for patent first in India, but MUST obtain NBA approval before the grant of the patent.
2. Foreign Applicants / Entities with foreign equity: Must obtain prior approval before filing the patent application.
3. Application Form: Form III (Application for seeking prior approval of NBA for applying for intellectual property right).
4. Fee: Statutory fee of Rs. 500 per application.
5. Benefit Sharing Agreement: NBA executes an agreement stipulating benefit sharing (typically 0.2% to 1.0% of ex-factory gross sales if commercialized) into the National Biodiversity Fund.
source: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), Chennai

TKDL Prior Art Formulation: Ashwagandhadi Churna (Charaka Samhita)
Classical Formulation Prior Art
Authority: CSIR-TKDL & Ministry of Ayush
Jurisdiction: IN

TKDL Identifier: CSIR-TKDL-AY-2001-001.
Classical Source: Charaka Samhita, Chikitsa Sthana, Adhyaya 2 (Vajikarana Adhyaya).
System of Medicine: Ayurveda.
Formulation: Ashwagandhadi Churna.
Ingredients: Ashwagandha root (Withania somnifera), Vidarikanda tuber (Pueraria tuberosa), Shatavari root (Asparagus racemosus), processed with Goghrita (cow ghee).
Traditional Indication: Balya (strength promoting), Rasayana (rejuvenator), and Dhatuposhaka (nourishment of body tissues).
Patent Prior Art Significance: This classical composition is established prior art under Section 3(p) of the Indian Patents Act, 1970. Any patent application claiming a simple herbal mixture of Ashwagandha with Shatavari and Vidari without unexpected synergistic bioassay proof is liable to be rejected based on this TKDL record. CSIR-TKDL access agreements with USPTO, EPO, and JPO allow patent examiners to cite this reference as anticipatory prior art.
source: CSIR-TKDL & Ministry of Ayush

authority: CSIR-TKDL & Ministry of Ayush

TKDL Prior Art Formulation: Haridra Khanda (Bhaishajya Ratnavali)
Classical Formulation Prior Art
Authority: CSIR-TKDL & Ministry of Ayush
Jurisdiction: IN

TKDL Identifier: CSIR-TKDL-AY-2002-089.
Classical Source: Bhaishajya Ratnavali, Sheetapitta Chikitsa Prakarana.
System of Medicine: Ayurveda.
Formulation: Haridra Khanda (Brihat).
Ingredients: Pure Rhizome powder of Haridra (Curcuma longa), fried in cow ghee (Go-Ghrita), boiled with milk (Godugdha) and sugar candy, fortified with Trikatu (Sunthi, Maricha, Pippali), Trijataka (Twak, Ela, Patra), and Vidanga.
Traditional Indication: Sheetapitta (urticaria), Udarda (allergic skin lesions), Kandu (pruritus), and Kotha (erythema).
Patent Defense Context: Following the revocation of the US Turmeric Patent (US Patent 5,401,504) by CSIR, this formulation was systematically indexed in TKDL. Claims for using turmeric extracts with black pepper (piperine) for anti-allergic or anti-inflammatory conditions are directly anticipated by this classical record under Section 3(p) of the Patents Act, 1970 unless non-obvious nanocarrier delivery or unexpected synergy is clinically established.
source: CSIR-TKDL & Ministry of Ayush
